title: the Toyol, the Thief's Spirit
summary: A small green goblin summoned by black magic to steal for its master, but the Toyol steals not just gold, but the master's humanity, one theft at a time.
full_text:
The Toyol is small. It is the size of a newborn child, curled and green-skinned, with pointed ears and red eyes that catch the light like embers. It has sharp teeth, and it smells of earth and iron.

The Toyol is not born. It is made. A bomoh makes the Toyol from a stillborn child. He takes the body and performs the ritual: the incantations, the offerings, the binding of the spirit to the earth.

The Toyol serves its master. If the master commands it to steal, it steals. The Toyol steals well. It is small, fast, silent. It slips through locked doors, slips under beds, slips into pockets.

But the Toyol steals more than gold. Every time the Toyol steals, it steals a piece of its master's soul. The piece that makes a person honest. The piece that makes a person feel guilty.

The master does not notice. He sees the gold. He does not see his soul disappearing. He does not notice his hands getting colder, his eyes getting darker, his laughter getting quieter.

After enough thefts, the master has no soul left. He is empty. He is a shell. He walks and talks, but there is nothing inside.

The bomoh who made the Toyol knows this. He knows the Toyol is a trap. But the bomoh makes Toyols. That is what he does.
moral: The things that steal for you are also stealing from you.
source: Malay/Singaporean oral tradition, documented by William Shellabear

title: the Pontianak, the Vampire Bride
summary: A beautiful woman in white who appears on lonely roads at night, her long black hair hiding a face that is not a face, because in Singapore beauty is the deadliest weapon.
full_text:
The Pontianak appears on lonely roads. She is beautiful. She wears a white dress, the white of a wedding dress, the white of a burial shroud. Her hair is black, long, falling to her waist. Her skin is pale, the pale of moonlight.

She looks lost. She looks lonely. She looks like a woman who needs help. The man who stops for her sees her face. She turns. She smiles. And the smile is wrong. The smile is too wide. The teeth are too sharp.

She strikes with her nails, long, curved, sharp as razors. She attacks with the force of a woman who has been dead for centuries and has nothing to lose.

The only defense against the Pontianak is the nail. A common iron nail driven into the roof of the house. The Pontianak cannot enter a house with a nail in the roof.

The Pontianak was once a woman who died on her wedding night. The grief did not die with her. The grief became the Pontianak.

If you see a woman in white on a lonely road at night, do not stop. Drive past. Drive fast. Do not look back.
moral: Beauty on a lonely road is not always what it seems.
source: Malay/Singaporean horror folklore, documented by Richard Winstedt

title: the Orang Bunian, the Hidden People
summary: A race of invisible beings who live alongside humans in the same forests and villages, visible only to those with the gift, because in Singapore the world is wider than you can see.
full_text:
The Orang Bunian are the hidden people. They live in the same world as humans. They walk the same roads, sit under the same trees, breathe the same air. But they are invisible. You can only see them with the gift.

The gift is rare. One in a thousand people has it. The gifted can see the Orang Bunian standing in the market, sitting in the mosque, walking through the forest. They see them as real as any person, but slightly transparent, slightly luminous.

The Orang Bunian are not spirits. They are a race who have lived in the Malay world since before the humans arrived. They were here first. They built the first villages, cleared the first forests.

Sometimes the Orang Bunian take human lovers. A gifted person may be chosen. They live together for a time. But the Orang Bunian do not age. The human does. After years the human is old and the Orang Bunian is still young. The Orang Bunian leaves.

The gifted smile. They know better than the ungifted. They have seen the Orang Bunian walking through the forest. The world is wider than you can see.
moral: The world is wider than your eyes can see.
source: Malay/Singaporean folklore, documented by Siti Hawa Salleh

title: the Bukit Timah Monkey Man
summary: A half-man half-monkey creature that lurks in the dense forest of Bukit Timah, stealing fruit and scaring hikers, because even in a city of five million the jungle remembers.
full_text:
The Bukit Timah Monkey Man lives in the forest. Not the forest that was. The forest that remains. A thin strip of primary rainforest on the slopes of Bukit Timah, the highest point on the island, where the trees are old and the undergrowth is thick and the monkeys chatter in the canopy.

The Monkey Man is not a monkey. It walks upright. It is the size of a man, but its body is covered in brown fur. Its face is simian, with a flat nose and deep-set eyes. Its hands are long, its fingers are nimble, its feet grip the branches.

The Monkey Man was seen first in the 1890s, when the British were building roads through the forest. The workers saw it at dusk, standing on the path, watching them. They threw stones. The Monkey Man climbed a tree and vanished.

It was seen again in the 1940s, during the Japanese occupation. Soldiers patrolling the forest heard a sound like laughter, but not human laughter. They followed the sound and found nothing. Only footprints in the mud, footprints that were too long to be human and too narrow to be ape.

It was seen again in the 1980s, by joggers on the Bukit Timah Nature Reserve trail. A figure stood on the path, motionless, watching them pass. They slowed. They looked. The figure was gone.

The Monkey Man does not attack. It does not speak. It watches. It stands at the edge of the clearing, at the bend in the path, at the place where the forest is thickest. It watches the humans walk through its forest.

The forest is shrinking. The buildings are closing in. The Monkey Man watches from the trees as the concrete creeps closer.

It does not leave. The jungle remembers. The Monkey Man remembers. The forest was here first.
moral: Even in a city, the jungle remembers who was here first.
source: Singapore urban folklore, documented in Straits Times archives

title: the Saka, the Possessing Spirit
summary: A spirit that attaches itself to a family line, growing stronger with each generation, demanding offerings that escalate from flowers to blood, because in Singapore some debts are inherited.
full_text:
The Saka does not haunt houses. It haunts bloodlines.

It attaches itself to a family, to a specific person in that family, and it stays. It passes from parent to child, from generation to generation, growing stronger with each transfer.

The Saka begins small. A dream. A whisper. A feeling of being watched. The person it attaches to feels a presence, a weight, a coldness that comes and goes without pattern.

The Saka asks for offerings. At first, the offerings are simple. A bowl of rice. A cup of water. A flower. The person leaves the offering at the edge of the house, at the door, at the window. The Saka accepts. The presence fades. The dreams stop.

But the Saka grows. It is a spirit that feeds on devotion. The more it receives, the more it wants. The offerings escalate. Rice becomes meat. Water becomes blood. Flower becomes sacrifice.

The person who carries the Saka cannot refuse. The Saka is part of the bloodline now. It is as much a part of the family as the name, as the house, as the face in the mirror.

The only way to remove the Saka is to transfer it. A bomoh can transfer the Saka to an object — a stone, a piece of cloth, a lock of hair. The object must be buried, hidden, forgotten. If the object is found, the Saka returns.

Some families have carried the Saka for generations. They do not speak of it. They do not explain the offerings at the door, the candles at the window, the silence that falls when the Saka is hungry.

The Saka waits. It is patient. It has time. It has generations.

The family serves.
moral: Some debts are inherited, and some spirits are passed down like names.
source: Malay/Singaporean spiritual tradition, documented by bomoh practitioners

title: the Toyol and the Jeweler
summary: A jeweler in Kampong Glam who used a Toyol to steal diamonds from his competitors, until the Toyol stole the one thing the jeweler treasured more than gold, his reflection.
full_text:
There was once a jeweler in Kampong Glam who could not compete. His rivals had bigger shops, better stones, wealthier customers. He had a small stall and a smaller reputation.

The jeweler went to a bomoh. He asked for a Toyol. The bomoh warned him. The bomoh always warns. But the jeweler was desperate, and desperate men do not listen.

The Toyol was made. The jeweler fed it with drops of his own blood. The Toyol obeyed. It stole diamonds from the rival shops. It slipped through locked doors, past guards, past alarms. It brought the diamonds to the jeweler.

The jeweler prospered. His shop grew. His reputation grew. His rivals shrank. He was happy. He fed the Toyol more blood. The Toyol stole more diamonds.

But the Toyol was hungry. It wanted more than blood. It wanted the piece of the soul that makes a person recognize themselves. The piece that lets you look in a mirror and know that the face looking back is yours.

One morning, the jeweler looked in the mirror and saw nothing. The mirror was clean. The glass was clear. But the face was gone. He looked at his hands. They were his hands. He touched his face. It was his face. But in the mirror, there was only the room behind him.

He ran to the bomoh. The bomoh shook his head. The Toyol has taken your reflection, the bomoh said. It cannot be returned. You gave it your blood. The Toyol took your face.

The jeweler lived the rest of his life without a reflection. He could not look in mirrors. He could not see himself in windows. He could not catch his face in the surface of still water.

He had the diamonds. He had the shop. He had the reputation. But he had no face.

The Toyol moved on. It found a new master. It stole new things. It took new pieces of new souls.

The jeweler died. No one came to the funeral. No one remembered his face. He had no reflection to leave behind.
moral: When you trade your soul for gold, the gold outlasts the soul.
source: Singapore urban folklore, Kampong Glam district

title: the Pontianak of the Coast
summary: A Pontianak who haunts the coastal roads of eastern Singapore, appearing as a woman with a baby, because in Singapore the sea and the dead are never far apart.
full_text:
The coastal road that runs along the eastern shore of Singapore is long and straight. On one side, the sea. On the other, the scrub and the old kampong houses that have not yet been demolished.

The Pontianak of the Coast appears here. She appears as a woman carrying a baby. The baby is wrapped in white cloth. The woman's hair is wet, as if she has just come from the sea. Her dress is wet too, and it clings to her body, and the water drips from the hem.

She walks along the road, holding the baby. She does not look at the cars that pass. She does not look at the people who walk. She looks at the baby. She talks to the baby. She sings to the baby.

The people who hear the song feel a coldness. Not the cold of the sea wind, but the cold of something that has no warmth. The cold of something that is not alive.

The Pontianak was a woman who drowned. She was a woman who went into the sea and did not come back. She was a woman who held her baby as the water rose, and the baby did not survive, and the woman did not survive, and the sea took them both.

The Pontianak carries the baby because the baby cannot carry itself. The baby is dead. The baby has always been dead. The Pontianak holds the baby because that is what mothers do.

The only defense against the Pontianak of the Coast is the scent of pandan leaves. The Pontianak cannot bear the smell. If you carry pandan leaves in your car, the Pontianak will not approach. If you hang pandan leaves on your door, the Pontianak will not enter.

The fishermen of the eastern coast still carry pandan. They hang it from the rearview mirror. They place it in the glove compartment. They wrap it in cloth and tuck it in their pockets.

The Pontianak walks. The baby sleeps. The sea is quiet.

The pandan leaves keep the cold away.
moral: A mother's love does not end at the water's edge.
source: Singapore coastal fishing community oral tradition
